newsitem.title: PERU: Peru mediators see "real progress" in hostage talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru mediators see "real progress" in hostage talks.

text.p: The Peruvian government and Marxist rebels holding 72 men captive at the Japanese ambassador's home are due to meet again on Saturday to try to draft an agenda for negotiations to end peacefully the 60-day Lima hostage drama.

Crisis mediators said the government and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) made "real progress" on Friday when they swapped lists of items they want on the agenda for definitive talks to free the hostages.

"The guarantors and observers consider the conversations have resulted in real progress. The conversations will continue tomorrow (Saturday)," Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent said, reading a statement to reporters through a megaphone.
No time was given for the start of Saturday's talks.
Vincent, part of a guarantors commission mediating the talks, said Friday's meeting at a house across the street from the residence was positive but added: "So far, the agenda has not been agreed."

Friday's three-hour meeting ended at dusk when a white Red Cross car shuttled the rebel representative believed to be MRTA No. 2 Rolly Rojas back across the street to the besieged diplomatic compound.
It was the second meeting between Rojas and government negotiator Domingo Palermo since Tuesday, when the two sides ended weeks of deadlock and restarted face-to-face talks broken off on Dec. 28.
The crisis erupted on Dec. 17 when a band of about 15 heavily armed rebels stormed a cocktail party and seized hundreds of guests. All but 72 mostly middle-aged VIP men have been released.
Despite Friday's apparent progress in talks, and growing concern about the health of the hostages as weeks in captivity drag by, a peaceful solution is not expected to come soon.
Since the residence was siezed, Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori has flatly rejected the MRTA's main demand of freedom for some 400 jailed comrades in exchange for the hostages' lives.
As Friday's talks got under way, Fujimori returned to Lima from a trip to the northeastern jungle town of Pucallpa, where he handed police six river patrol boats and inaugurated an electrical plant.
He refused to comment on the negotiations.
Although Saturday's talks will be the third face-to-face meeting in five days, details of the discussions are scarce.

Speaking publicly about the talks for the first time on Thursday, Education Minister Palermo said Tuesday's discussions were "quite positive" but that the government was "very worried" about the overall situation.
"We will continue our work, and then we hope to have results," he said.

Among those still held in the mined and booby-trapped residence are two Peruvian government ministers, Japan's and Bolivia's envoys, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and Fujimori's brother, Pedro.
The hostages have spent Christmas, New Year and now Valentine's Day away from their loved ones.
On Friday, a few miles from the siege, in the "Park of Love" on the Pacific coast, 72 couples were married at a mass wedding to show solidarity with the 72 captives.
"We are here to tell them they are not alone," said Mayor Oscar Barron at the end of the ceremony held beneath a huge statue of two lovers embracing, called "The Kiss."

Hostages also enjoyed Valentine's Day chocolates sent into the residence by wives and girlfriends, although some probably did not indulge as they have taken to dieting and exercising to lose weight, according to doctors allowed into the compound for check-ups.

"Although some of them go jogging on the second floor, because of the lack of physical exercise some have put on weight and have decided to go on a diet," said Dr. Miguel Sanchez, a released hostage himself. "Some have lost 13 to 18 pounds (six to eight kg)."
A heart specialist, Sanchez told Peruvian television that on his latest visit on Thursday he found the hostages calm and in generally good health.

One Peruvian human rights group on Friday made a special award to Roman Catholic priest Juan Julio Wicht Rossel, a hostage who was offered his freedom by the MRTA early in the siege, but who decided to stay on to look after the spiritual well-being of his fellow captives.
